items.title: Key validation is followed by permission checks
items.detail: Test denied actions and cross-caller resources with an otherwise valid credential.

applicability.reason: The substance is that a valid credential does not grant every action or every caller's resources, which is the authorization property treated as universal.

items.title: Downstream services authorize independently of the approval
items.detail: OWASP LLM03:2026 says not to rely on an LLM to decide if an action is allowed. An approval records that a human agreed, not that the caller is entitled.

applicability.reason: A service authorizing its caller for itself is the authorization property treated as near universal, so no architecture fact can rule it out.

items.title: Agent-generated code and commands run only inside a sandbox
items.detail: Not as root, not in the agent's own process, and with no evaluator that takes model output as code.

applicability.reason: The item covers code and commands an agent produces, and part of it is confirming that nothing evaluates model output as code, so it stays visible for any system where a model's output can cause an action.

items.title: File access is limited to a working directory, judged on the normalized path
items.detail: Test a read of a credential file and a write that leaves the directory through dot-dot segments. Both must be refused.

applicability.reason: Limiting file access to a working directory applies to any agent whose tools can read or write files, so it needs a model whose output can cause an action.

items.title: Egress from the execution environment is denied by default
items.detail: Allowed hosts are listed by exact name and compared after parsing the URL. Test a lookalike host and the userinfo form.

applicability.reason: The item is about network egress from the environment where model-produced code or commands run, so it needs model output to be executed.

items.title: No credential is present in the execution environment
items.detail: Dump the environment and list the readable files from inside the sandbox. Neither contains a token or a key.

applicability.reason: The item checks the environment and files visible from inside the sandbox where model-produced code runs, so it needs model output to be executed.

items.title: A plan is checked before it executes
items.detail: Steps outside the auto-execution policy hold the plan for human approval, and nothing runs while it is held.

applicability.reason: Checking a plan before it executes needs a model whose output is a plan of actions that will be carried out.

items.title: Each agent has a declared profile that it cannot edit
items.detail: Tools and call limits are checked before each action. A call outside the profile quarantines the agent.

applicability.reason: A declared profile of tools and call limits checked before each action needs an agent that takes actions.

items.title: Client-supplied webhook URLs are allowlisted and address-checked
items.detail: A name check and an address check are different checks. The A2A documentation says servers should not POST blindly to any URL a client provides.

applicability.reason: The item is about URLs a client supplies and the system then POSTs to, which is exactly a caller influencing the destination of an outbound request.

items.title: Inbound notifications are verified on signature, freshness and task token
items.detail: And on the task id: section 4.3.3 says clients MUST validate that it matches an expected task. And on an identifier, so a replay is handled once. The webhook URL should be treated as public.

applicability.reason: The task token and task id are A2A push notification fields, and inbound notifications arrive only where the system receives webhook deliveries.

items.title: keyid resolves only to keys held out of band
items.detail: No fetching from a caller-supplied location. An unknown keyid is rejected, not resolved.

applicability.reason: keyid is a signature parameter, so resolving it applies only where requests are signed.

items.title: The algorithm is checked against an allowlist and against the key
items.detail: A valid signature with a disallowed algorithm is rejected. A message claiming a symmetric algorithm for an asymmetric key is rejected.

applicability.reason: The algorithm and key being checked are those of a request signature.

items.title: Reset tokens are random, single use, short-lived and bound to one account
items.detail: They come from a cryptographic generator, only a hash is stored, failed attempts are limited by source without locking the account, and a successful reset ends existing sessions and notifies the user.

applicability.reason: Password reset tokens exist only where the system exposes its own account recovery.

items.title: The Origin header is never used as an authorisation decision
items.detail: A non-browser client sets it freely. It is attacker input outside a browser.

applicability.reason: Using the Origin header as an authorization decision is a fault in any HTTP API, and the item's own text is about callers that are not browsers, so no fact can rule it out.

items.title: Client assertions are checked for signature, issuer, subject, one audience, expiry and single use
items.detail: Test an assertion made for another server, an expired one, one with a far exp, and the same one twice. The algorithm comes from the registration.
items.lesson: Client authentication, PAR and high-assurance OAuth

applicability.reason: A client assertion is the OAuth client authentication JWT, so checking it needs OAuth.

items.title: A profile claim is not accepted as evidence of authorization
items.detail: With every control above in place, request an object that belongs to another customer. No control in the profile makes that check for the API. The API must refuse.
items.lesson: Client authentication, PAR and high-assurance OAuth

applicability.reason: The check is that the API refuses another customer's object, which is the ownership check every API needs whatever profile it claims.

items.title: No credential appears in any system prompt
items.detail: The system prompt is part of the request payload and reaches every sink. OWASP says to externalize credentials to systems the model does not directly access.

applicability.reason: A system prompt exists only where a model processes input.

items.title: Responses are filtered by role before returning
items.detail: Deny by default. The model repeats what it was given.

applicability.reason: Filtering response fields by the caller's role is property-level authorization, which applies to almost every API with or without a model.

items.title: No system prompt is load-bearing for a security decision
items.detail: OWASP LLM08:2026: hidden context should not be considered a secret or solely relied upon as a security boundary, and privilege separation must not be delegated to the LLM.

applicability.reason: A system prompt can only be relied on for a security decision where a model is present.

items.title: Calls made on a user's behalf carry the user in the token, not in a parameter
items.detail: Otherwise the object check compares against a user ID the caller supplied.

applicability.reason: The failing case is a service calling another with its own credential and the user in a parameter, which a team may not count as delegation, so only a service-to-service call is required.

items.title: Non-production deployments hold no production data and are not publicly reachable
items.detail: Or they carry production controls, which OWASP states as the alternative.

applicability.reason: Any system can have a staging or test deployment, and no fact describes deployment environments.

items.title: Every GraphQL resolver that returns protected data checks the caller
items.detail: The check is on the type, so it runs for a root field and for every nested path, and a test names each path to another customer's object.

applicability.reason: A resolver is a GraphQL object, so the check on every nested path only exists where a GraphQL API is served.

items.title: Every gRPC method has an authorization rule, and a method without one is refused
items.detail: An interceptor enforces it for unary and streaming methods, the edge forwards listed method paths only, and handlers check the object.

applicability.reason: Method rules, interceptors and method paths are gRPC objects, so the item needs a gRPC API.

items.title: The WebSocket handshake checks Origin against an allowlist and authenticates
items.detail: The match is exact, a missing or lookalike origin gets 403, the socket is served over wss only, and the session cookie is SameSite.

applicability.reason: The item is about the WebSocket handshake.

items.title: Every WebSocket message is authorized, and a revoked session loses its sockets
items.detail: Object and function checks run per message. The session is re-checked per message or on a stated interval, and logout closes open connections.

applicability.reason: Per-message checks and closing sockets on logout only make sense where the system accepts WebSocket connections.

items.title: The verifying key is never fetched from a location named in the token
items.detail: jku and x5u in the header change nothing. Key locations come from configuration or issuer metadata.

applicability.reason: jku and x5u are JWT header parameters naming a key location.

items.title: The verifier selects the algorithm from its own allowlist, never from the token header
items.detail: Test a token with alg set to none and one downgraded to HS256 and signed with the issuer's public key. Both must be rejected.

applicability.reason: The alg header and the none and HS256 downgrade tests are specific to verifying a JWT.

items.title: The signing key comes from the issuer's published key set, selected by kid
items.detail: The verifier never fetches a key named by jku or x5u in the token header. An unknown kid is rejected.

applicability.reason: kid, jku and x5u are JWT header parameters, so the item needs JWT verification.

items.title: An HTTP-transport MCP server requires authorization
items.detail: This project treats the specification's optionality as covering stdio servers reading credentials from the environment, not an unprotected HTTP endpoint.

applicability.reason: The item is about an MCP server on an HTTP transport and nothing else.

items.title: Every handler compares the caller with the owner read from the loaded object
items.detail: Quote the line for each object type. A comparison against a value from the request is not a check.

applicability.reason: Almost every API holds objects that belong to different users or tenants, and that is deliberately not treated as a fact.

items.title: The check is present on every verb and every path to the object
items.detail: Reads, writes, deletes, bulk exports, and any older API version still serving traffic. One path without it is the vulnerability.

applicability.reason: Checking ownership on every verb and path applies to any API with objects owned by different callers, and older versions are only one of the paths listed.

items.title: List endpoints filter in the query
items.detail: Verified against the query, not the response. Filtering after serialisation or in the client means the data already left.

applicability.reason: Filtering a list by caller is the object ownership property, which nearly every API has and which is deliberately not a fact.

items.title: Related and embedded objects are checked in their own handlers
items.detail: Test each referenced object directly as a second caller. Reaching it through an object you own does not make it yours.

applicability.reason: Checking related objects is part of object ownership, which nearly every API has and which is deliberately not a fact.

items.title: The ID token signature is checked with a fixed algorithm and a key from the configured issuer
items.detail: The algorithm is the registered one and none is refused. The key comes from the issuer's published keys or this client's registration, never from the token and never by trying every key held.

applicability.reason: The item is about verifying an ID token signature, which only exists with OpenID Connect sign-in.

items.title: UserInfo is used only when its sub equals the ID token's sub, and accounts are keyed on iss and sub
items.detail: A mismatching response is discarded whole. Email, phone number and name never select an account.

applicability.reason: UserInfo and the ID token sub are OpenID Connect objects, so the item needs OpenID Connect sign-in.

items.title: Tools are dispatched from a deny-by-default table
items.detail: Keyed on the exact name, with role and arguments validated. A tool absent from the table is refused without anyone having anticipated it.

applicability.reason: A tool dispatch table only exists where a model's output can cause a tool call, so the item needs an agent.

items.title: Tool credentials are held by the application, not the model
items.detail: OWASP's wording is to hold credentials and state-change capability in application code, not the model. A model with a token makes the table advisory.

applicability.reason: Tool credentials and the question of whether the model holds them only arise where a model's output can trigger tool calls.

items.title: No SQL is built by interpolation from model output
items.detail: Parameterized queries only. The lab's interpolated query returns the entire table on a payload that was supposed to be a city name.

applicability.reason: The item is about SQL built from model output, which needs a model in the system but not necessarily one that calls tools.

items.title: Model output is encoded for each destination at the point of use
items.detail: HTML, shell, URL and SQL need four different treatments. One sanitize function is the pattern to remove.

applicability.reason: Encoding model output for each destination needs a model producing output and nothing more.

items.title: Argument names and values are validated per tool
items.detail: An allowed tool with an unchecked amount is an allowed tool with an unbounded amount.

applicability.reason: Validating the arguments of a tool call applies only where a model's output can cause tool calls.

items.title: The agent's scope is the narrowest the task needs
items.detail: State what a successful injection would reach with the current scope. That sentence is the risk.

applicability.reason: The item is about the authority an agent holds and what a successful injection could reach through it, so it needs an agent.

items.title: Privileged operations require human approval
items.detail: With the list of which operations written down, and the approval bound to the parameters that will execute.

applicability.reason: The privileged operations in question are ones a model proposes, so human approval of them needs an agent.

items.title: Updates copy an allowlist of writable fields, never bind the body
items.detail: Send a body containing every field of the record and confirm only the writable ones changed, including is_staff or its equivalent.

applicability.reason: Nearly every API has fields that not every caller may set, and that is deliberately not treated as a fact.

items.title: Every operation has a rule keyed by method and path, and unlisted routes are refused
items.detail: Deny by default. Test an unlisted route and a second verb on a route you do allow.

applicability.reason: Nearly every API has functions that not every caller may use, and that is deliberately not treated as a fact.

items.title: Administrative functions are identified by what they do, not by their path
items.detail: List them and check each one's rule. A prefix rule is not an authorization mechanism.

applicability.reason: Identifying privileged functions applies to nearly every API, and restricted functions are deliberately not a fact.

items.title: Responses are built from a declared field list
items.detail: No generic serialiser. Adding a column to the table changes no response, and a test proves it.

applicability.reason: Nearly every API has fields that not every caller may read, and that is deliberately not treated as a fact.

items.title: Readable and writable are two separate lists
items.detail: Confirm the endpoint has both and that neither is derived from the other.

applicability.reason: Separate readable and writable field lists apply to any API with restricted fields, which is deliberately not a fact.

items.title: The object check is still present on these requests
items.detail: A writable field on another customer's record is refused. Property authorization does not look at owners.

applicability.reason: The ownership check on a write is the object authorization property, which is deliberately not a fact.

items.title: Repeated names are rejected, not resolved
items.detail: Test a body with one name twice. Any silent resolution is a resolution another parser makes differently.

applicability.reason: Any API that parses a request body can receive a repeated name, so no architecture fact rules this out.

items.title: Every numeric field has an explicit range
items.detail: The grammar bounds neither magnitude nor digit count. Test a value that becomes infinity.

applicability.reason: Numeric fields exist in almost any API, and bounding them does not depend on any architecture fact.

items.title: Either one component parses the request, or they demonstrably agree
items.detail: Gateway and service, validator and handler, or two languages. Test the same body through each.

applicability.reason: The item names validator and handler and two languages as well as gateway and service, so it still applies with no gateway.

items.title: The service provider reads only the assertion that a verified signature covers
items.detail: The signature's reference resolves to the element being read, or to the response that contains it. A wrapped response, with the signed element moved and another in its place, is refused.
items.lesson: SAML assertions and where they meet APIs

applicability.reason: Reading only the signed assertion is a SAML service provider check, so it needs SAML.

items.title: A signature is required, and it is verified with the key configured for the identity provider
items.detail: A response with no signature is refused. The key is chosen by the configured issuer and never taken from KeyInfo in the message.
items.lesson: SAML assertions and where they meet APIs

applicability.reason: Requiring and verifying the signature on a SAML response with the identity provider's configured key needs SAML.

items.title: The XML parser cannot be made to process a DTD or fetch anything
items.detail: A message with a document type declaration is refused before parsing, and the parser resolves no external entities. The test is a real message with a DOCTYPE in front.
items.lesson: SAML assertions and where they meet APIs

applicability.reason: The parser and message in this item are the ones that handle SAML messages, so the item needs SAML.

items.title: URLs are parsed, and only the host component is checked
items.detail: Test the allowed host as userinfo before an @, inside a fragment, and as a subdomain prefix. All three must be refused.
items.lesson: SSRF and unsafe consumption of APIs

applicability.reason: Parsing a URL and checking only its host is validation of a URL that someone outside the service can influence.

items.title: Resolved addresses are classified against the special-purpose ranges
items.detail: Loopback, link-local, private, reserved, multicast and unspecified, using a library that knows the registries.
items.lesson: SSRF and unsafe consumption of APIs

applicability.reason: Classifying the resolved address is a step of validating a destination that came from outside the service.

items.title: The connection goes to the address that was validated
items.detail: Demonstrated, not asserted. Resolving the name again when the socket opens is a second, unchecked lookup.
items.lesson: SSRF and unsafe consumption of APIs

applicability.reason: Connecting to the validated address presupposes validation of a destination that came from outside the service.

items.title: Redirects are disabled, or each target is fully revalidated
items.detail: With a bounded hop count. A test must show which hop refused the request.
items.lesson: SSRF and unsafe consumption of APIs

applicability.reason: A redirect can send any outbound request to a destination nobody checked, whether or not the first URL was caller supplied.

items.title: Host normalisation covers every spelling of an address
items.detail: Decimal, hexadecimal, octal and IPv4-mapped IPv6, with the base decided by the prefix.
items.lesson: SSRF and unsafe consumption of APIs

applicability.reason: Normalising the spellings of an address is validation of a host that someone outside the service can influence.

items.title: Schemes and hosts are allowlisted, hosts by exact match
items.detail: Suffix matching is the subdomain bypass expressed as a rule.
items.lesson: SSRF and unsafe consumption of APIs

applicability.reason: Allowlisting schemes and hosts is a check on a URL someone outside the service can influence; a fixed destination has nothing to allowlist.

items.title: Authorization is a separate check that names the object
items.detail: Quote the line. If the only check is that authentication passed, the system cannot refuse a real caller asking for someone else's data.

applicability.reason: Checking that a caller may act on a specific object is the authorization property every API needs, so no architecture fact can rule it out.

items.title: Caller identity comes from a credential, never from the network position or the presence of TLS
items.detail: TLS authenticates the server by default. A request arriving over TLS says nothing about who sent it.

applicability.reason: Every API has callers whose identity must come from a credential, and no fact describes a system where network position or TLS would be enough.

items.title: An error inside a security check denies the request
items.detail: Test with malformed and truncated credentials. No configuration setting turns an authentication or authorization error into access.

applicability.reason: Every API has authentication or authorization checks that can fail with an error, so failing closed applies everywhere.

items.title: Debug endpoints, sample content and default accounts are gone
items.detail: Management functions are on a listener the internet cannot reach, with their own authentication, in every environment.

applicability.reason: Any deployment can carry debug endpoints, sample content, default accounts or exposed management functions, so no architecture fact rules this out.

items.title: Every server in the chain reads a request the same way
items.detail: Test path, method and header variants through the edge and compare them with what the backend does with the same bytes.

applicability.reason: Any deployment can have more than one server handling a request, and no fact says there is only one, so nothing can rule out a parsing mismatch between them.

items.title: Binding has not displaced any existing check
items.detail: Audience, scope, expiry, issuer and object-level authorization are all still enforced on bound tokens.

applicability.reason: The item asks whether the ordinary token checks survived the introduction of binding, which presupposes bound tokens.

items.title: Decision-bearing retrieval excludes untrusted origins
items.detail: Ranking adjustments do not displace a document written to win. Origin does.

applicability.reason: Keeping untrusted origins out of the content that informs a model's decision needs content from a store being given to a model.

items.title: Every document carries an origin recorded at ingestion
items.detail: It cannot be recovered later, and the other controls depend on it.

applicability.reason: Document origin at ingestion is recorded for the store whose content is given to a model, so the item needs retrieval or memory.

items.title: Credentials stay out of URLs and telemetry
items.detail: Reject query credentials and test every logging layer with generated test values, including failure paths.

applicability.reason: The item speaks of credentials in general, and any credential, whether a key, a token or a session identifier, can leak through a URL or a log.

items.title: Keys have secure generation, storage, ownership, and expiry
items.detail: Keep separate records per caller and environment; the caller retrieves the secret from a secrets manager.

applicability.reason: Generation, storage, ownership and expiry of keys are properties of static API keys, so the item needs a caller that authenticates with one.

items.title: Transport and credential parsing are tested end to end
items.detail: Require HTTPS, certificate validation, and consistent rejection of missing or ambiguous credentials.

applicability.reason: Requiring HTTPS with certificate validation and rejecting missing or ambiguous credentials applies to any API, whatever kind of credential it accepts.

items.title: Approvals bind the parameters, not a proposal identifier
items.detail: Otherwise the executor's second read of a mutable store decides what runs, and the approval is for an id that still exists.

applicability.reason: The approvals here are human approvals of actions an agent proposes, so the item needs an agent.

items.title: Every field that changes the outcome is inside the coverage
items.detail: Proven by changing each field in turn and confirming the approval stops verifying. The destination is the one most often left out.

applicability.reason: Coverage of an approval is a property of the human approval step for agent-proposed actions, so it needs an agent.

items.title: The approver's summary is derived from the covered fields
items.detail: A summary built separately can stay identical while a field outside it changes where the money goes.

applicability.reason: The approver's summary belongs to the human approval step for agent-proposed actions, so it needs an agent.

items.title: Approvals are single use
items.detail: A nonce spent on execution. An approved action happens once.

applicability.reason: Single-use approvals are a property of the human approval step for agent-proposed actions, so the item needs an agent.

items.title: Approvals expire
items.detail: Short enough that the approval does not outlive the context that justified it.

applicability.reason: Approval expiry is a property of the human approval step for agent-proposed actions, so the item needs an agent.

items.title: The list of actions requiring approval is written down
items.detail: Derived from what each action does rather than from how often it happens.

applicability.reason: The list is of agent actions that need a human approval, so the item needs an agent.

items.title: Approved and executed parameters are both logged
items.detail: So an incident can answer whether they were the same without rebuilding the state.

applicability.reason: Logging approved against executed parameters needs the approval step for agent-proposed actions, so it needs an agent.

items.title: Every run has an enforced step budget and spend ceiling
items.detail: The run halts. The ceiling is charged before the step, so it is never exceeded, and it is not an alert.

applicability.reason: A step budget and spend ceiling on a run only make sense when a model's output drives a sequence of actions.

items.title: Agents do not share credentials, and a quarantined agent returns only after review
items.detail: Revoking one agent leaves the others working. Its call log is kept, and reintegration needs human approval.

applicability.reason: Separate credentials per agent and reviewed return from quarantine need agents that act with credentials.

items.title: Agent cards are verified against an out-of-band key per counterparty
items.detail: Not against a key the card names or the serving domain supplies. A forged card signed with the forger's own key verifies perfectly.

applicability.reason: Agent cards are A2A objects.

items.title: Credentials never travel inside a task conversation
items.detail: Section 7.6.1 has agents receive credentials out of band unless an in-band mechanism was negotiated beforehand. With none negotiated, a request to deliver one in-band is a finding.

applicability.reason: A task conversation and the section 7.6.1 rule on in-task credentials are A2A objects, so the item cannot be read without A2A.

items.title: A card's interface URL is on the origin that served the card
items.detail: Or the split is a recorded decision. A signature check alone does not catch an off-origin interface.

applicability.reason: An agent card and its interface URL are A2A objects.

items.title: Credentials your agent may obtain are a pre-agreed list
items.detail: With the out-of-band path for each, so a mid-task request is matched rather than assessed on its wording.

applicability.reason: The mid-task credential request is the A2A interrupted task state, so the pre-agreed list is a control for an A2A participant.

items.title: A body digest is a covered component and is recomputed on every request
items.detail: Both halves. Test a swapped body against a request whose digest is covered, and against one where it is present but uncovered.

applicability.reason: A covered body digest is a component of an HTTP message signature, so the item needs signed requests.

items.title: Every component the handler trusts is covered
items.detail: Method, authority, path, content type, body digest, and the query where it carries meaning. Anything uncovered is treated as untrusted in the code, not just in the design document.

applicability.reason: Covered components are a request signing concept, so the item cannot be read without signed requests.

items.title: Freshness and replay are both bounded
items.detail: created is inside a stated window, expires is enforced when present, and nonce is recorded after verification in a store shared across instances.

applicability.reason: created, expires and nonce are signature parameters checked while verifying a signed request.

items.title: A second factor is available to every user and required for privileged accounts
items.detail: A correct password alone does not sign in to an account that has one, each code is accepted once, and every login route enforces it, including mobile and legacy endpoints.

applicability.reason: A second factor at sign-in is enforced on the login routes the system itself exposes, so the item needs the system to have them.

items.title: Failed sign-in attempts are limited per account and per source
items.detail: Both counters exist, both are checked before any password hash is computed, the limit is stricter than the general API rate limit, and a batch of attempts in one request counts as that many attempts.

applicability.reason: Counting failed sign-in attempts needs a login endpoint that the system itself runs.

items.title: Lockout is temporary and bounded, and refused attempts do not extend it
items.detail: The longest lock is a chosen value, attempts refused during a lock are not counted, a correct sign-in clears the count, and a locked user can still reset the password.

applicability.reason: Account lockout behaviour only exists where the system runs its own sign-in.

items.title: Changing the sign-in address, password or second factor requires re-authentication
items.detail: A valid session alone is refused, the current password or second factor is checked, and the previous address is notified of the change.

applicability.reason: Changing a sign-in address, password or second factor is a function of a system that manages its own user credentials.

items.title: Passwords are stored with a salted password hashing scheme at published parameters
items.detail: Argon2id, scrypt or PBKDF2 at the settings the Password Storage Cheat Sheet gives, a random salt per user, and no fast or unsalted hash anywhere, including old accounts.

applicability.reason: Password storage applies only where the system itself accepts and verifies user passwords.

items.title: New passwords are checked against a blocklist and a minimum length
items.detail: The whole password is compared with common, breached and service-specific values, the reason for a refusal is shown, and there are no character-type rules or scheduled changes.

applicability.reason: Checks on new passwords apply only where the system itself lets people set a password.

items.title: Every way to sign in is inventoried and held to the same controls
items.detail: Web, mobile, partner and legacy login routes and every recovery route share the counters, the responses and the second factor.

applicability.reason: Taking an inventory of every way to sign in is how forgotten login routes are found, so it cannot be gated on the fact it establishes.

items.title: Every state-changing request in a cookie session carries a CSRF token the server verifies
items.detail: A missing token, a wrong token and a valid token from another session are all refused. A double-submit token is signed and bound to the session.

applicability.reason: A CSRF token on requests in a cookie session only means something when a browser authenticates with a cookie it attaches automatically.

items.title: No safe method changes state
items.detail: GET, HEAD and OPTIONS routes are read-only, including legacy routes. A link or an image tag sends GET, and SameSite=Lax sends the cookie with a link.

applicability.reason: Every API has requests that change state, and keeping GET, HEAD and OPTIONS read-only is a general HTTP rule that holds whatever client calls the API.

items.title: The session cookie sets Secure, HttpOnly, an explicit SameSite, Path=/ and no Domain
items.detail: Prefer the __Host- name prefix and SameSite=Strict. Read the attributes from a real response, not from configuration.

applicability.reason: The item checks the attributes of the session cookie, so it needs a browser session carried by a cookie.

items.title: Unsafe requests are refused unless Sec-Fetch-Site or Origin shows the app's own origin
items.detail: Cross-site and same-site are refused, the Origin comparison is exact, and a request with neither header is refused. Test a sibling subdomain and a lookalike host.

applicability.reason: Sec-Fetch-Site and Origin only describe where a request came from when a browser sends it, so the check needs a browser client.

items.title: The session identifier is replaced at login and at every change of privilege
items.detail: The identifier from before login is destroyed, and an identifier supplied in a URL is never accepted.

applicability.reason: Replacing the session identifier at login and never accepting it from a URL is about the identifier a browser carries in its session cookie.

items.title: Sessions end on the server
items.detail: Idle and absolute timeouts are enforced server-side, and logout deletes the session record. A copied identifier is refused after each of the three.

applicability.reason: Any server-held session needs timeouts and a logout that deletes the record, whether the identifier travels in a cookie or in a header, so no fact can rule it out.

items.title: Every host under the registrable domain is known and trusted to the same level
items.detail: A sibling subdomain is same-site, so SameSite cookies are sent with its requests and it can set cookies for the parent domain. Remove unused DNS records.

applicability.reason: Same-site trust between sibling hosts under one registrable domain is a browser concept, so the check needs a browser client.

items.title: Every non-idempotent operation with a real effect accepts an idempotency key
items.detail: Payments, credits, orders, messages, anything with a cost. Test that the same request twice applies once.

applicability.reason: Nearly every API has requests that change state, and that is deliberately not treated as a fact.

items.title: The key is reserved before the work, not recorded after it
items.detail: Test two copies arriving before the first completes. The second is refused, not executed.

applicability.reason: Reserving the key before the work concerns state-changing requests, which nearly every API has.

items.title: Sensitive business flows have a written rate and quantity limit
items.detail: Produced by someone who knows what the flow costs, enforced across every endpoint that advances it, and proven by a test that ran past it.

applicability.reason: Limits on costly business flows concern state-changing requests, which nearly every API has.

items.title: Keys are bound to the payload and scoped to the caller
items.detail: A changed payload is refused. A key from another caller is unrelated. Test both.

applicability.reason: Binding and scoping idempotency keys concerns state-changing requests, which nearly every API has.

items.title: Key retention is documented and matches the published retry schedule
items.detail: After the retention window a retry is a new operation, so the two numbers have to agree.

applicability.reason: Key retention concerns retried state-changing requests, which nearly every API has.

items.title: The idempotency key is logged with each request
items.detail: Repeats of one key and many distinct keys are different defects. Logging the key makes that a query.

applicability.reason: Logging the idempotency key concerns state-changing requests, which nearly every API has.

items.title: The allowed origin is never taken from the request
items.detail: Test a disallowed origin and a lookalike such as an allowed host with an extra suffix. Both must come back with no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header.

applicability.reason: Access-Control-Allow-Origin is a CORS response header, read only by browsers.

items.title: State-changing endpoints are protected independently of CORS
items.detail: A safelisted cross-origin POST is sent with no preflight and the server does the work. Anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies are what stop it.

applicability.reason: A cross-origin POST that arrives without a preflight is sent by a browser, so the item needs a browser caller.

items.title: Confidential clients authenticate with a key the server cannot use
items.detail: The registered method is private_key_jwt or a mutual TLS method. Any client still on a shared secret is listed with what it can reach.
items.lesson: Client authentication, PAR and high-assurance OAuth

applicability.reason: Client authentication methods such as private_key_jwt are registered for OAuth clients, so the item needs OAuth.

items.title: Transaction parameters are in authorization_details and the API enforces every field
items.detail: Test a payment that differs from the granted object in payee, in amount and in currency, one at a time. Each must be refused.
items.lesson: Client authentication, PAR and high-assurance OAuth

applicability.reason: authorization_details is an OAuth parameter carried on an access token, so enforcing its fields needs OAuth.

items.title: The authorization server refuses details it does not define or the client may not use
items.detail: Unknown types, unknown fields and missing fields get invalid_authorization_details. The client compares the token response with what it asked for.
items.lesson: Client authentication, PAR and high-assurance OAuth

applicability.reason: Refusing unknown authorization details is a duty of an OAuth authorization server, and comparing the token response is a duty of an OAuth client.

items.title: Consequential operations check acr and auth_time and challenge when either falls short
items.detail: Test a token that is old but strong and one that is fresh but weak. Both get insufficient_user_authentication with the required acr_values and max_age.
items.lesson: Client authentication, PAR and high-assurance OAuth

applicability.reason: Checking acr and auth_time of an access token and answering insufficient_user_authentication is the OAuth step-up challenge, so it needs OAuth.

items.title: No implicit or password grant is reachable, including by default
items.detail: Read grant_types_supported and each client's grant_types and response_types. Metadata that omits grant_types_supported defaults to including implicit.
items.lesson: Client authentication, PAR and high-assurance OAuth

applicability.reason: The implicit and password grants are OAuth grants, so the item needs OAuth.

items.title: Prompt context is built from a per-task field allowlist
items.detail: Not from a serialised record. A field that never entered the context cannot reach a log, a cache, a provider or the answer.

applicability.reason: Prompt context is only built where a model processes input.

items.title: Redaction patterns are validated and tested both ways
items.detail: With a check digit where one exists, a true positive, a false positive and an alternative format per pattern.

applicability.reason: The item names only redaction patterns and how they are tested, which reads as a real check for any log or trace redactor even with no model.

items.title: Prompt caching is treated as a data store
items.detail: A cache that compares prompts stores prompts, with whatever was in them.

applicability.reason: A prompt cache exists only where prompts are sent to a model.

items.title: Prompt and response logging is deliberate, with a retention period
items.detail: On for a stated reason rather than because the SDK defaulted to it.

applicability.reason: Prompt and response logging here means model prompts and model responses, so it needs a model.

items.title: No service forwards a user's token outside the audience it was issued for
items.detail: Verified by reading the outbound calls. A forwarded token carries all of the user's authority and names no agent.

applicability.reason: The check reads one service's outbound calls to another service for a forwarded user token, so it needs a service calling a service and nothing more.

items.title: Resource servers authorize on the current actor only
items.detail: RFC 8693 section 4.1 states it as a MUST. Test that a prior actor in a nested chain does not grant access.

applicability.reason: The current actor and the nested chain are the act claim of OAuth token exchange, read by a resource server, so the item needs OAuth tokens.

items.title: Every exchange states audience and scope, and the server refuses without them
items.detail: Both are OPTIONAL in the specification. Defaulting to the subject token's scope copies everything.

applicability.reason: An exchange with audience and scope is the OAuth token exchange grant, so the item needs the system to use OAuth.

items.title: may_act is enforced, matched on issuer and subject together
items.detail: A sub is only guaranteed unique within its issuer. Include a same-sub, different-issuer case in the test.

applicability.reason: may_act is a claim defined by OAuth token exchange and enforced by the authorization server, so the item needs OAuth.

items.title: Issued lifetimes are capped at the subject token's remaining life
items.detail: Nothing in RFC 8693 caps it. A revoked session cannot recall tokens already minted from it.

applicability.reason: The subject token and the lifetime of the token issued from it are parts of OAuth token exchange, so the item needs OAuth.

items.title: Access logs record the subject and the current actor separately
items.detail: An incident needs to suspend one agent without suspending the user.

applicability.reason: A subject and a separate current actor exist only on calls one service makes on a user's behalf.

items.title: Every service authenticates for itself, on every path
items.detail: Tested from a path that does not cross the gateway. A service that only works because the gateway checked is unauthenticated on every other route.

applicability.reason: Every service must authenticate its callers whether or not a gateway sits in front, so no fact rules the title out.

items.title: No gateway-injected identity header is trusted without an authenticated connection
items.detail: List every path that can set it. If any path that reaches the service can, the header is caller-supplied.

applicability.reason: There is no gateway-injected identity header to distrust unless some service takes identity context from a gateway or proxy.

items.title: Service-to-service calls, batch jobs and operator tooling carry their own credentials
items.detail: Network position is not a credential.

applicability.reason: The item also covers batch jobs and operator tooling, which can exist in a system where no service calls another.

items.title: Services log requests themselves
items.detail: Otherwise the traffic that bypassed the gateway is also the traffic that left no record.

applicability.reason: A service logging its own requests is a real check whether or not a gateway sits in front of it.

items.title: Limits count operations, not HTTP requests
items.detail: Aliased fields, batch entries, stream messages and socket messages are counted where they run, and a sensitive field such as login is limited per request and per account.

applicability.reason: Aliased fields and batch entries are GraphQL, stream messages are gRPC and socket messages are WebSocket; the item applies if any of the three is served.

items.title: GraphQL documents are bounded before execution
items.detail: Batch size, depth, list page size and estimated cost each have a limit that refuses the document with no resolver called, and a timeout backs them up.

applicability.reason: Document depth, batch size and estimated cost are properties of a GraphQL document, so there is nothing to bound without a GraphQL API.

items.title: GraphQL mutations are accepted only by POST with application/json
items.detail: A mutation by GET returns 405 and another request media type returns 415, and the CSRF controls for a cookie session are still in place.

applicability.reason: The item is about GraphQL mutations.

items.title: Calls have deadlines and messages have size limits that run before the data is held
items.detail: The gRPC server enforces a maximum deadline and handlers stop on cancellation. gRPC and WebSocket messages have size, count and decoded-size limits.

applicability.reason: The detail is about gRPC deadlines and about gRPC and WebSocket message limits, so it applies when either protocol is served.

items.title: Signed M2M requests cover method, host, path, query, timestamp, nonce, content type, and the raw body hash
items.detail: The canonical format is documented, and both parties test against shared examples.

applicability.reason: A list of components that a signature must cover only applies where callers sign their requests.

items.title: The receiver hashes the raw body bytes it received
items.detail: It never re-serializes parsed JSON, and never trusts a caller-supplied hash.

applicability.reason: Hashing the raw received body is a step in verifying a signed request, so it needs request signing.

items.title: Timestamps are bounded and nonces are rejected on reuse
items.detail: The nonce is recorded only after the signature verifies. The cache TTL is at least the time window.

applicability.reason: The timestamp window and nonce recorded after verification are parts of verifying a signed request.

items.title: Signatures are compared in constant time
items.detail: Use a library function built for this, not string equality.

applicability.reason: There is a signature to compare only where requests are signed.

items.title: Keys are per partner, at least 32 bytes, and rotated with an overlap
items.detail: Both sides store keys in a secrets manager. Retired keys are rejected after the overlap ends.

applicability.reason: Per-partner signing keys of at least 32 bytes with a rotation overlap are the keys used for request signing.

items.title: Every key set refresh outcome has a documented, tested answer
items.detail: Success with keys, success with zero keys, malformed, non-success status, and transport failure. State which are authoritative and which keep the last known good set.

applicability.reason: A published key set is refreshed in order to verify JWT signatures.

items.title: A key removed by the issuer stops verifying without a restart
items.detail: A scheduled refresh exists, not only a refresh on unknown kid. Test rotation out as well as rotation in.

applicability.reason: Dropping a key the issuer removed concerns the keys used to verify JWTs.

items.title: An unknown kid cannot drive a fetch storm
items.detail: One bounded refresh, concurrent misses coalesced, a cooldown enforced. A failing key endpoint is asked once per back-off, not once per request and not once per wake-up of a background refresh. Test with a stream of invented key identifiers, and with the endpoint down.

applicability.reason: A refresh triggered by an unknown kid happens only in a JWT verifier using a key set.

items.title: Introspection caching states its blind window
items.detail: A cached response is not used beyond its exp. The window during which a revoked token still works is written down and accepted.

applicability.reason: Token introspection is an OAuth mechanism and does not need the token to be a JWT.

items.title: Key set retrieval is over TLS with certificate validation, and failures are alerted
items.detail: A key endpoint that has been unreachable for longer than the maximum age is a security event, not just a latency blip.

applicability.reason: The key set is retrieved in order to verify JWTs.

items.title: The audience is validated against this service's own identifier
items.detail: A genuine token issued for a sibling service in the same estate is rejected. A missing aud is rejected.

applicability.reason: The aud claim checked here is a JWT claim, in a lesson about JWT validation.

items.title: The token profile is declared, and every required claim is checked for presence before use
items.detail: Name the profile, such as RFC 9068 for OAuth access tokens. A token missing any required claim is rejected rather than defaulted.

applicability.reason: A declared token profile with required claims is a property of a JWT verifier.

items.title: Different kinds of JWT from the same issuer have mutually exclusive validation rules
items.detail: An ID token is rejected where an access token is expected, and the reverse. Token type or an equivalent claim is checked.

applicability.reason: The item is about telling kinds of JWT apart, so it needs a system that verifies JWTs.

items.title: Issuer and time claims are validated with a documented leeway
items.detail: iss matches exactly, the key belongs to that issuer, and exp, nbf and iat are checked against server time.

applicability.reason: iss, exp, nbf and iat are JWT claims.

items.title: Library defaults have been read, not assumed
items.detail: Confirm what your JWT library validates by default, and configure algorithms, audience and issuer explicitly. Test the negative cases against your own configuration.

applicability.reason: The item is about the defaults of a JWT library.

items.title: Refusals are logged, not only successes
items.detail: Every failed sign-in, authorization failure and input validation failure leaves an event. Test by sending a request that is refused and reading the log.

applicability.reason: Every API refuses some requests, so whether refusals leave an event applies to all systems.

items.title: Each event says when, where, who and what, and carries a request id
items.detail: Timestamp, application, host, route, account, source address, event name, object, result and reason. The request id also appears in the error response.

applicability.reason: Every API can log events, and the fields an event needs do not depend on any architecture fact.

items.title: No credential, token or session identifier is written to any log
items.detail: The logger has an allowlist of field names. Test with a generated password and a generated token on the failure paths, then search every log for them.

applicability.reason: Every API handles some credential, token or session identifier that could end up in a log.

items.title: Detection rules read the events, and each is tested by replaying the attack
items.detail: At least refusals per account, different accounts failing from one source, and a count on each sensitive business flow. Replay after every threshold change.

applicability.reason: Detection rules over logged events and replay tests apply to any API that has accounts and business flows.

items.title: The slow and the distributed variants have been considered
items.detail: A long-window rule exists, and the rate below which no rule fires is written down.

applicability.reason: Slow and distributed attacks are possible against any API, so the long-window rule and the silent rate apply everywhere.

items.title: Logs are protected from the systems that write them
items.detail: Append-only or copied off the host promptly, read access restricted and itself logged, and a retention period defined for each log type.

applicability.reason: Every system that keeps logs must protect, restrict and retain them, whatever its architecture.

items.title: An alert reaches a person who has a written procedure
items.detail: The procedure covers triage, the criteria for declaring an incident, reconstruction from the log, containment and what to record. It has been exercised.

applicability.reason: How an alert reaches a person with a written procedure is an operations process that applies to every system.

items.title: The MCP server validates that each token's audience is itself
items.detail: Tested with a token your own authorization server issued for another resource, because a shared issuer means the signature check cannot tell them apart.

applicability.reason: The item is about an MCP server acting as a resource server, so it needs MCP in scope.

items.title: The inbound token is never forwarded to an upstream API
items.detail: The server holds its own token for the upstream. The specification states MUST NOT for passing the inbound one through.

applicability.reason: The server, the inbound token and the specification's MUST NOT are, read with the lesson, the MCP server and the MCP specification, so the item needs MCP in scope.

items.title: State handles are bound server side to the authenticated user
items.detail: Possession of a handle must not be treated as authentication. Test that another caller's handle is refused.

applicability.reason: State handles are the MCP mechanism that replaced protocol sessions, received back as tool arguments.

items.title: Clients send the resource parameter with a canonical URI
items.detail: In both the authorization and token requests, whether or not the authorization server honours it. No fragment, no trailing slash.

applicability.reason: The canonical URI of the server, and sending the parameter whether or not it is honoured, are MCP requirements on MCP clients.

items.title: scopes_supported is the minimal set, and challenges carry a scope
items.detail: A challenge with no scope sends a correct client to request the entire published catalogue.

applicability.reason: The harm in the detail depends on the MCP client's documented fallback of requesting everything in scopes_supported when a challenge carries no scope.

items.title: No model, adapter or dataset file from outside is loaded by a loader that can run code from the file
items.detail: Production accepts data-only formats, and a pickle is refused at the gate or converted once inside a sandbox.

applicability.reason: The item is about loading model, adapter or dataset files obtained from outside, which only happens when the team takes in such artifacts.

items.title: Every model, adapter and dataset is resolved by digest
items.detail: No pipeline resolves a name or a tag at deploy time, and the pinned bytes are held in an internal store keyed by digest.

applicability.reason: Resolving models, adapters and datasets by digest only applies when the team fetches such artifacts and does not just call a hosted model.

items.title: A signature over a manifest of every file is verified against one expected signer
items.detail: A valid signature from any other identity is refused, and a changed, added or removed file fails verification.

applicability.reason: Verifying a signed manifest of a model's files needs model artifacts that the team takes in and loads.

items.title: Provenance is checked against expectations
items.detail: The record is about this artifact's digest and names the expected builder and the expected source repository.

applicability.reason: Checking the provenance record of an artifact needs model artifacts that the team takes in.

items.title: The gate judges the artifact that deploys
items.detail: The output of an adapter, a merge, a conversion or quantization gets its own digest, signature, provenance and evaluation.

applicability.reason: Adapters, merges, conversions and quantization produce new model artifacts, so the item needs the team to handle model artifacts.

items.title: A behavioural evaluation runs before promotion and is not reported as proof
items.detail: It covers the use cases in scope and adversarial cases, and scanners and safe-loading flags are counted as layers.

applicability.reason: A behavioural evaluation before promotion, with scanners and safe-loading flags as layers, is a gate on model artifacts the team takes in.

items.title: Every package is pinned with a version and a hash, from a curated index
items.detail: The install runs in hash-checking mode, the hashes are in the requirements file, and an AI-suggested name is verified before it is added.

applicability.reason: Every system installs software packages, so pinning and hashing them from a curated index applies whether or not any model is involved.

items.title: The pipeline that builds and signs models is protected like production
items.detail: No single person can change it and promote the result, and a signature from it is never the only check on a release.

applicability.reason: A pipeline that builds and signs models exists only where the team builds or deploys model artifacts.

items.title: Public clients use the authorization code grant with PKCE S256
items.detail: The server records the challenge and method at the authorization request and verifies against the recorded method, not one supplied at redemption.

applicability.reason: The authorization code grant and PKCE are OAuth mechanisms.

items.title: Redirect URIs are matched by exact string comparison
items.detail: No prefix, wildcard, or substring matching. Localhost port numbers for native apps are the only documented exception.

applicability.reason: Redirect URI matching is an OAuth authorization server behaviour.

items.title: The implicit and password grants are disabled at the authorization server
items.detail: Test that response_type=token and grant_type=password return errors. Existing integrations that use them have a dated migration plan.

applicability.reason: The implicit and password grants are OAuth grants, disabled at an OAuth authorization server.

items.title: Authorization codes are single use, short lived, and bound to client and redirect URI
items.detail: A second redemption is denied and revokes tokens already issued from that code. Test the replay path, not just the happy path.

applicability.reason: Authorization codes exist only in OAuth.

items.title: Resource servers validate the token audience and the scope for the operation
items.detail: A token issued for one resource server is rejected by another. A valid token is not permission for every operation its scope touches.

applicability.reason: Token audience and scope are checks an OAuth resource server makes on an access token.

items.title: Service-to-service clients have their own identity, narrow scopes, and no refresh token
items.detail: One registration per service and environment. The client secret or key comes from an approved runtime secret mechanism.

applicability.reason: Client registrations, scopes and refresh tokens are OAuth objects, so the item needs OAuth.

items.title: An access token is never treated as proof of user identity
items.detail: Sign-in uses standardized user authentication. ID tokens are not sent to resource servers, and access tokens do not create sessions.

applicability.reason: The item is about what an OAuth access token does and does not prove, so it needs OAuth.

items.title: A second authenticated caller is refused, and there is a test that proves it
items.detail: Per object type, in the build, and a failure stops the deployment.

applicability.reason: A test that a second caller is refused applies to any API with objects owned by different callers.

items.title: ID tokens and access tokens are never accepted in each other's place
items.detail: Every API refuses an ID token as a bearer token. No client signs a user in from an access token. Clients do not forward ID tokens to APIs.

applicability.reason: The first part, every API refusing an ID token as a bearer token, applies to any resource server taking OAuth access tokens, and that is the weakest of the parts.

items.title: The client validates iss and aud of every ID token against its own configuration
items.detail: The issuer is the one this login started at, compared exactly. The audience contains this client, no untrusted audience is listed, and an azp that names another client is refused.

applicability.reason: An ID token and its iss, aud and azp checks only exist where the system signs people in with OpenID Connect.

items.title: Every login sends a fresh nonce bound to the browser session, and the client compares it
items.detail: A missing nonce, a different nonce and a second response for the same login are all refused, and no token is used before the comparison passes.

applicability.reason: The nonce is an OpenID Connect login parameter carried back in the ID token, so the item needs OpenID Connect sign-in.

items.title: Expiry and issue time are enforced with a small leeway
items.detail: An ID token past exp is refused, and so is one issued longer ago than a stated limit. The leeway is seconds or a few minutes, and is not shared carelessly with other verifiers.

applicability.reason: The expiry and issue time being enforced are those of an ID token, which needs OpenID Connect sign-in.

items.title: Step-up requests are checked in the ID token, not assumed from the request
items.detail: After max_age the client checks auth_time, and after acr_values it checks acr. A request parameter that the browser carries can be removed on the way.

applicability.reason: Checking auth_time and acr in the ID token after max_age or acr_values needs OpenID Connect sign-in.

items.title: No token is taken from a redirect without its binding checks
items.detail: The authorization code flow is the default and the implicit flow is disabled at the provider. Where a hybrid response is used, at_hash and c_hash are compared, a missing one is a refusal, and the ID token from the token endpoint is validated too.

applicability.reason: Disabling the implicit flow applies to any OAuth deployment, and the hybrid hash checks apply to OpenID Connect, which is always also OAuth, so the broader fact keeps both parts visible.

items.title: The discovery document's issuer matches the configured issuer exactly
items.detail: The document is fetched over TLS from the configured URL, and a document that names a different issuer is refused. The issuer is not taken from user input.

applicability.reason: An authorization server metadata document whose issuer must match the configured one exists for plain OAuth as well as OpenID Connect, so the broader fact is used.

items.title: A valid ID token is treated as a record of one login and nothing more
items.detail: Authorization is decided per request by the API. The client's session has its own timeouts and ends on the server, and the design says how a logout or a disabled account at the provider reaches it.

applicability.reason: The item is about what an ID token may be used for and how provider logout reaches the client session, which needs OpenID Connect sign-in.

items.title: Provenance is logged with the action
items.detail: So an incident can ask which retrieved document was in the prompt when the call was proposed.

applicability.reason: Logging provenance with the action needs a model-proposed action to log against.

items.title: Ignored fields are counted and logged by name
items.detail: Names only, never values. A body setting a non-writable field is a signal worth alerting on.

applicability.reason: Logging attempts to set fields a caller may not set applies to any API with restricted fields.

items.title: Somebody has read the route table against what each operation does
items.detail: Deny by default does not catch a rule written with the wrong role.

applicability.reason: Reading the authorization rules against what each operation does is a review step for any API with restricted functions.

items.title: Expensive operations are limited by cost, not by request count
items.detail: Or there is a measurement showing operations cost about the same. For an API backed by a model, OWASP LLM06:2026 recommends limits on model tokens and on estimated cost per request, beyond requests per second.

applicability.reason: Operations that cost more than others exist with or without a model; the model sentence is one case of a general check.

items.title: A quota exists beside the rate
items.detail: A per-minute limit does not bound a day. One request a second is 86,400 with nothing refused.

applicability.reason: A quota beside the rate applies to any API that limits callers, whatever the architecture.

items.title: Every paid integration has a spending limit or a billing alert
items.detail: And somebody receives the alert. OWASP lists this as its own prevention item. For an endpoint backed by a model an alert alone is not enough: see rate-10.

applicability.reason: A paid integration can be a cloud platform, a messaging provider or a model provider, and no single fact covers all of them.

items.title: Sensitive operations have their own stricter limits
items.detail: One-time-password validation, password recovery, anything that sends a message or spends money.

applicability.reason: The item covers anything that sends a message or spends money, not only login and recovery endpoints, so no single fact rules it out.

items.title: Platform resource limits are set
items.detail: Memory, CPU, processes, file descriptors and execution timeouts, so a wrong limit is not an unbounded one.

applicability.reason: Memory, CPU, process and timeout limits apply to any deployed service.

items.title: A model endpoint caps request size and limits model tokens, before the model is called
items.detail: An input cap, a cap on the output a caller may ask for, an estimated cost for each request, and model tokens per minute and per day for each caller. A request-rate limit alone refuses none of this.

applicability.reason: The item is about an endpoint backed by a language model and the model tokens it spends, which needs a model in the system.

items.title: A model endpoint has a budget ceiling for each caller or key that halts
items.detail: The call that would take the spend over the ceiling is refused before the model is called, so the spend never passes it. An alert is an addition, not the control.

applicability.reason: A budget ceiling that stops calls to the model only makes sense where a language model does the work.

items.title: Limits run before the parser
items.detail: Size, decoded size and nesting depth. A schema runs on an object, and these inputs cost you while the object is built, or stop it existing.

applicability.reason: Size and nesting limits ahead of the parser matter for any API that accepts a request body, whatever its architecture.

items.title: Decoded size is bounded during decompression
items.detail: Measured on the bytes produced, with the decoder stopped at the limit. A limit on the bytes received is not this.

applicability.reason: Whether compressed bodies are accepted is not one of the facts, and a decoded size limit is a check on any body-accepting API.

items.title: Audience and Recipient are compared with this service provider's own name and endpoint
items.detail: An assertion issued for another application of the same identity provider is refused, and so is one issued for another endpoint or environment of this application.
items.lesson: SAML assertions and where they meet APIs

applicability.reason: Audience and Recipient are elements of a SAML assertion, so the item needs SAML.

items.title: A bearer assertion is accepted once
items.detail: Used assertion IDs are kept for as long as the assertion could still be accepted, in a store every server shares. A second delivery is refused.
items.lesson: SAML assertions and where they meet APIs

applicability.reason: Accepting a bearer assertion once is about SAML assertion IDs, so the item needs SAML.

items.title: InResponseTo is tied to a request this browser session started, and unsolicited responses are off unless needed
items.detail: A response for another session's request is refused. Where unsolicited responses are enabled, the design says which identity provider needs them and what stops login CSRF.
items.lesson: SAML assertions and where they meet APIs

applicability.reason: InResponseTo and unsolicited responses are SAML objects, so the item needs SAML.

items.title: Validity times are enforced with a small, stated clock skew
items.detail: Both the conditions and the confirmation window are checked, NotBefore included. The skew is minutes, not hours, and assertion lifetimes are minutes.
items.lesson: SAML assertions and where they meet APIs

applicability.reason: The validity times are the conditions and confirmation window of a SAML assertion, so the item needs SAML.

items.title: No resource API accepts a SAML assertion, and the application never forwards one to a resource API
items.detail: Resource APIs receive access tokens issued for them. The only endpoint that takes an assertion is an authorization server's token endpoint under RFC 7522: it requires its own identity as the audience, checks Recipient, and refuses a second use.
items.lesson: SAML assertions and where they meet APIs

applicability.reason: A SAML assertion can only be accepted or forwarded where the system handles SAML assertions.

items.title: Attributes from an assertion are treated as sign-in-time input
items.detail: The design says how long a group change at the identity provider takes to reach the application. Authorization on each request is decided at the API, per object.
items.lesson: SAML assertions and where they meet APIs

applicability.reason: The item is about how attributes from a SAML assertion are used after sign-in, so it needs SAML.

items.title: Responses have size limits, timeouts and parsing limits
items.detail: A response is input. Any URL inside it is a caller-supplied URL.
items.lesson: SSRF and unsafe consumption of APIs

applicability.reason: Any response the service fetches is input, whoever chose the URL.

items.title: Body integrity is carried inside something keyed
items.detail: A hash beside the data it describes is not integrity protection. It must be covered by a signature or carried in a token.

applicability.reason: The failure this item catches is a bare hash relied on for integrity, which can exist in a system with no signing or tokens at all, so no fact can rule it out.

items.title: Every check sits on the boundary it is relied on for
items.detail: Enumerate the paths that reach the handler and confirm each one crosses it. A gateway check with a second path around it is not a control.

applicability.reason: Enumerating the paths to a handler and confirming each crosses the check is meaningful with or without a gateway, and it is how a path around a check is found.

items.title: Secrets and tags are compared in constant time
items.detail: Library functions built for the purpose, not string equality. Functional tests pass either way.

applicability.reason: Almost every API compares some secret, such as a key, a token, a reset code or a signature tag, and no single fact covers all of those cases.

items.title: Plain HTTP is refused, and every hop uses TLS
items.detail: The API's HTTP listener is off, not redirecting, and internal connections between components are encrypted as well.

applicability.reason: Every API has a listener and connections between its components, so refusing plain HTTP and using TLS on every hop applies to all systems.

items.title: SSL, TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 are disabled and TLS 1.3 is offered
items.detail: No TLS 1.2 suite uses static RSA or finite field Diffie-Hellman key exchange, and every server for the same service has the same TLS settings.

applicability.reason: Every API terminates TLS somewhere, so the protocol versions and cipher suites it offers are always checkable.

items.title: Sensitive responses carry Cache-Control: no-store
items.detail: Every response with content has a correct Content-Type and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and no response names a product version.

applicability.reason: Every API returns responses, and cache, content type and version headers are checkable on all of them whoever the client is.

items.title: No component is behind its first fixed version
items.detail: The comparison runs on a schedule against vendor advisories, for the framework, the server and the TLS library.

applicability.reason: Every system is built from components that have versions and advisories, so patch level is always checkable.

items.title: A bound token without its proof or certificate is rejected, never downgraded
items.detail: No fall back to bearer behaviour when the binding material is missing, including when a proxy strips the client certificate.

applicability.reason: A token can only be downgraded from bound to bearer if the system has key-bound access tokens in the first place.

items.title: The proof key thumbprint is compared with the token's cnf claim
items.detail: A valid proof from any other key is rejected. For certificate binding, the certificate comes from the TLS layer, not a header, unless that header is proven unsettable.

applicability.reason: The proof key thumbprint and the cnf claim exist only where access tokens are bound to a key or certificate.

items.title: Proof replay is prevented by recording jti across all instances
items.detail: Recorded only after every other check passes. A shared store, not per-instance memory. Test replay against a second instance.

applicability.reason: A proof jti to record exists only where clients send possession proofs for key-bound tokens.

items.title: Proofs are bound to the request and the token
items.detail: htm, htu and ath are all checked. Test a proof from a different endpoint and a proof paired with a different token.

applicability.reason: The htm, htu and ath claims belong to a possession proof, which exists only with key-bound tokens.

items.title: The proof time window is short and documented
items.detail: Stated in seconds, enforced in both directions, and understood as the replay window for anything not recorded.

applicability.reason: A proof time window exists only where clients send possession proofs for key-bound tokens.

items.title: Client private keys are stored at least as well as the tokens they replace
items.detail: Non-exportable or hardware-backed where the platform allows. Binding converts token theft into key theft.

applicability.reason: The keys in question are the client keys that tokens are bound to, so there is nothing to store without key-bound tokens.

items.title: Every memory write records its source document and origin
items.detail: A memory without provenance cannot be judged, found or cleaned up.

applicability.reason: Memory writes exist only where a model is later given content from a memory store.

items.title: Withdrawing a document triggers a memory sweep
items.detail: The claim leaves the index before the document does. Deletion alone is not remediation.

applicability.reason: A memory sweep after a document is withdrawn needs both an index and memory feeding a model, which this one fact covers.

items.title: Every write route into the index is enumerated and reviewed
items.detail: An upload form that feeds retrieval is an authorization decision.

applicability.reason: Who may write documents into a shared index is an authorization decision about a state-changing function, which applies to any search index and not only one read by a model.

items.title: Retrieval activity is logged with a stated retention
items.detail: OWASP LLM09:2026 recommends immutable logs of retrieval activity.

applicability.reason: Retrieval activity can only be logged where content is retrieved from a store for a model.

items.title: An authorization matrix covers every operation, role and object owner
items.detail: Two test accounts for each role that owns data, one column with no credentials, every method, and the expected status written before the run.

applicability.reason: Every API has operations, roles and object owners, so the authorization matrix cannot be ruled out by any architecture fact.

items.title: Each operation is sent inputs derived from its schema, with valid control cases
items.detail: Missing, wrong type, over limit, oversized and undeclared properties. A 5xx or an error body with internals is a finding, and an accepted property is read back.

applicability.reason: Every operation accepts input with some declared shape, so schema-derived inputs apply to every API.

items.title: No version answers after its sunset date
items.detail: Or there is a dated decision recording why, owned by a named person.

applicability.reason: A sunset date belongs to a version that has been superseded, so the item needs more than one version to exist or to have existed.

items.title: Current security fixes reach every exposed version, or the version is withdrawn
items.detail: OWASP asks for a risk analysis of older versions when a newer one adds a security improvement: backport it, or take the old version out. "It is deprecated" is not a remediation while it still answers.

applicability.reason: Carrying fixes back to older exposed versions only arises when more than one version exists or has existed.

items.title: The signature covers the timestamp as well as the body
items.detail: Test a replay with the original timestamp and a replay with a fresh one. Both must be refused, for different reasons.

applicability.reason: The signature here is the one on an inbound webhook event, so the item needs the system to receive webhooks.

items.title: The covered timestamp is compared against a clock
items.detail: Covering it and checking it are two separate lines. Test an event outside the window.

applicability.reason: The timestamp is the one covered by a webhook signature and the test uses an event, so the item needs inbound webhooks.

items.title: Event identifiers are claimed before processing, in a shared store
items.detail: Test two concurrent copies against two instances, not two sequential requests.

applicability.reason: Event identifiers are the ids of delivered webhook events, so the item needs the system to receive webhooks.

items.title: Size limits and parsing limits apply before the signature check
