items.detail: The endpoint is unauthenticated until the signature verifies, so the parser meets attacker input first.

applicability.reason: Limits ahead of the signature check concern an endpoint whose only authentication is the webhook signature, so it needs inbound webhooks.

items.title: One secret per sender, rotatable with an overlap
items.detail: A shared secret lets any sender forge as another.

applicability.reason: The secret is the one each webhook sender signs with, so the item needs the system to receive webhooks.

items.title: The endpoint URL is not treated as a secret
items.detail: And the event contents are treated as untrusted input, including any URL inside them.

applicability.reason: The endpoint URL and the event contents are those of a webhook receiver, so the item needs inbound webhooks.

items.title: Withdrawal revokes before it deletes the record
items.detail: Evidence that the credential is refused, dated after the revocation and before the record was removed.

applicability.reason: Withdrawing a credential in the right order applies to every kind of credential, so no architecture fact rules it out.

items.title: Every credential has a revocation route that someone has executed
items.detail: Tested on a credential you can afford to lose, before you need it on one you cannot.

applicability.reason: A tested way to revoke is needed for every kind of credential, so no architecture fact rules it out.

items.title: No credential is shared across systems, and none is unused
items.detail: One credential per system. Anything active and unused past the threshold is withdrawn or justified in writing.

applicability.reason: Shared and unused credentials can exist with any credential type, so no architecture fact rules it out.

items.title: The register stores no secret values, and scopes are recorded
items.detail: Metadata only. A credential whose scope was never recorded cannot be assessed.

applicability.reason: What the credential register holds is an inventory question that applies whatever kinds of credential exist.

items.title: Exposed keys can be revoked everywhere
items.detail: Measure the revocation bound across caches and confirm the old key fails while its replacement works.

applicability.reason: Revoking an exposed key across caches and issuing a replacement only makes sense where callers authenticate with static keys.

items.title: Session-wide approvals are recorded with the fields they constrain
items.detail: Zero is a legitimate answer and a legitimate finding.

applicability.reason: Session-wide approvals are approvals of agent actions, so the item needs an agent.

items.title: Output is validated between agents, behind a circuit breaker
items.detail: The checkpoint refuses unknown fields, out-of-range values and more items than the cap. The breaker opens on consecutive failures.

applicability.reason: Validating output passed from one agent to the next needs a model whose output triggers an action, here a message to another agent.

items.title: The kill switch revokes the agent's credential where it is accepted
items.detail: Evidence is a refused call made directly to the resource after the switch, not a record that the switch was used.

applicability.reason: A kill switch that revokes the agent's credential needs an agent that acts with a credential.

items.title: Declared skills are compared with the skills the endpoint answers
items.detail: The undeclared one is the one with no review behind it.

applicability.reason: Declared skills are the skills listed in an A2A agent card.

items.title: The public agent card contains nothing you would not publish
items.detail: Sensitive detail moves behind an authenticated extended card, and the card endpoint is access-controlled if its content warrants it.

applicability.reason: The public agent card exists only for an A2A server.

items.title: The targeted protocol version is recorded and reviewed
items.detail: A2A is versioned and still moving. A review against an older version can be wrong rather than merely stale.

applicability.reason: A process item, but its text limits it to recording the A2A protocol version, which has no meaning unless the system takes part in A2A.

items.title: A covered component missing from the message is a rejection
items.detail: The verifier does not substitute a blank value to complete the base.

applicability.reason: Rebuilding a signature base with a missing covered component only happens when verifying a signed request.

items.title: Key rotation works without a cutover
items.detail: A new keyid per key, both accepted during an overlap, and the retirement date recorded.

applicability.reason: Rotating by keyid with an overlap concerns the keys used to sign and verify requests.

items.title: The choice of symmetric or asymmetric is written down with its reason
items.detail: If an HMAC is still in use, the threat model states that a breached receiver forging as the caller is accepted.

applicability.reason: The choice between a shared secret and a key pair exists only where requests are signed.

items.title: Login, reset and registration answer the same for known and unknown accounts
items.detail: The status, body, headers and work are the same, and an unknown username reaches the 429 after the same number of failures as a real one.

applicability.reason: Uniform answers from login, reset and registration need the system to expose those endpoints.

items.title: Authentication failures, lockouts and resets are logged and alerted on
items.detail: The alerts cover one source failing across many accounts and many sources failing against one account, and a user is told when their password was right and the second factor was not.

applicability.reason: The failures, lockouts and resets to be logged come from the system's own sign-in and recovery endpoints.

items.title: Endpoints refuse content types they do not parse
items.detail: A JSON endpoint answers 415 to text/plain and form content types. This is a layer, not the CSRF defence.

applicability.reason: Any API endpoint can be sent a content type it does not parse, and refusing it is a general hardening layer that does not depend on the kind of client.

items.title: The place a browser app keeps its tokens is a recorded decision
items.detail: Tokens in script-readable storage are exposed to any injected script. A backend for frontend keeps them on the server and needs the CSRF controls above.

applicability.reason: The decision is about where an application running in a browser keeps its tokens, so it needs a browser client.

items.title: The stored response is replayed, including failures
items.detail: Not recomputed. A failed operation replays as the failure it was.

applicability.reason: Replaying the stored response concerns retried state-changing requests, which nearly every API has.

items.title: Origin comparison is on the serialised form
items.detail: Byte for byte, no trailing slash, scheme and port included. Test the same host over http and with a trailing slash.

applicability.reason: Comparing the Origin of a request against an allowlist is a CORS decision, and CORS only has an effect when a browser calls the API.

items.title: Vary: Origin is sent wherever the response depends on the origin
items.detail: Otherwise a shared cache can serve one origin's allowed response to another.

applicability.reason: Vary: Origin matters only where a response depends on the Origin of a CORS request, which presupposes browser callers.

items.title: Access-Control-Max-Age is set deliberately and bounded
items.detail: It defaults to 5 seconds and browsers clamp it. The value is how long a tightened policy keeps being ignored.

applicability.reason: Access-Control-Max-Age is read only by a browser's preflight cache.

items.title: Preflight responses are asserted in tests, not confirmed by hand
items.detail: Include a method the endpoint does not support, a request carrying Authorization, and a preflight answered with a redirect.

applicability.reason: A test item, but its text limits it to preflight responses, which only browsers request.

items.title: Pushed authorization requests are required, not just supported
items.detail: require_pushed_authorization_requests is set for the server or the client, and an authorization request with parameters on the URL is refused.
items.lesson: Client authentication, PAR and high-assurance OAuth

applicability.reason: Pushed authorization requests are an OAuth mechanism, so the item needs OAuth.

items.title: A request_uri is single use, short lived, unguessable and bound to its client
items.detail: Test a second use, a use after expires_in, a made-up value and a use with another client_id. Confirm the rightful client can still use it after the last one.
items.lesson: Client authentication, PAR and high-assurance OAuth

applicability.reason: A request_uri is the reference issued by an OAuth pushed authorization request, so the item needs OAuth.

items.title: Clients check the iss parameter of the authorization response
items.detail: A response whose iss is not the issuer the request went to is dropped before the code is redeemed. RFC 9700 requires a mix-up defense of any client that uses more than one authorization server.
items.lesson: Client authentication, PAR and high-assurance OAuth

applicability.reason: The iss parameter of the authorization response is an OAuth object checked by an OAuth client.

items.title: The sinks a prompt reaches are enumerated
items.detail: Request, logs, traces, caches, provider. Marked with which are yours and which have redaction before writing.

applicability.reason: The sinks a prompt reaches can only be listed where prompts are sent to a model.

items.title: Provider retention and training terms are recorded and dated
items.detail: A contractual fact that changes, not a property of your code.

applicability.reason: Model provider retention and training terms matter only where a model processes the system's data.

items.title: Delegation chain depth is bounded
items.detail: And the bound is small enough that exceeding it is a design question rather than an alert.

applicability.reason: A delegation chain exists only where services act for a user toward other services.

items.title: Missing information blocks a rule rather than passing it
items.detail: A checklist that passes when it does not know will reliably report that the system is fine.

applicability.reason: This is about how a review is run, so it applies to every review.

items.title: Unanswered questions are reported with the severity their rule carries
items.detail: Not downgraded for uncertainty, which would make the review quieter the less it knows.

applicability.reason: This is about how review results are reported, so it applies to every review.

items.title: The report states coverage: concluded, clean, blocked
items.detail: A reader assumes anything unmentioned was assessed and fine.

applicability.reason: A coverage statement belongs in every review report whatever the system looks like.

items.title: Findings are ordered worst first and grouped by origin
items.detail: Several findings in one area are usually one finding about that area.

applicability.reason: Ordering and grouping findings is review method and applies to every review.

items.title: Each open item is marked as a setting or a decision
items.detail: The decisions are the ones still open next quarter. Name them on day one.

applicability.reason: Marking open items as a setting or a decision is review method and applies to every review.

items.title: The rule table and the review date are version controlled
items.detail: So the next review of the same system is a diff rather than a repeat.

applicability.reason: Keeping the rule table and review date under version control is review method and applies to every review.

items.title: The path list comes from the network and is dated
items.detail: Connection logs, mesh telemetry or firewall rules. A diagram is the claim being tested, not the evidence.

applicability.reason: Listing every source that can connect to a service is an inventory step that makes sense with or without a gateway.

items.title: Every reachable non-current version has a retirement date
items.detail: Reachability is the test, not whether the gateway routes to it.

applicability.reason: A non-current version can only be reachable if an older version of the API has ever been exposed.

items.title: Each gateway control is recorded as present or absent per path
items.detail: Schema validation, size limits, rate limits and logging are absent on any path that skips the gateway. Say so explicitly.

applicability.reason: There are no gateway controls to record per path unless some service relies on a gateway or edge component for security.

items.title: Introspection, reflection and field suggestions are off unless the API is published
items.detail: Errors are generic, and no finding is closed on the grounds that an operation's name is hidden.

applicability.reason: Introspection and field suggestions belong to GraphQL and reflection belongs to gRPC, so the item applies when either protocol is served.

items.title: Monitoring reads the protocol's own outcome
items.detail: Alerts use grpc-status, GraphQL errors and per-message events, not the HTTP status, and each service logs refusals with the caller and the operation.

applicability.reason: Outcomes carried outside the HTTP status exist only in these three protocols.

items.title: Intermediaries do not alter signed components
items.detail: Gateway and proxy behavior is tested with signed requests end to end.

applicability.reason: Signed components exist only where requests are signed, and the test is what shows whether an intermediary changes them.

items.title: The shared-secret limitation is accepted in the threat model
items.detail: Otherwise use asymmetric request signatures.

applicability.reason: Accepting that the receiver of a shared secret can forge is a decision about request signing, and the item is how a reviewer learns whether the signing is symmetric.

items.title: A kid matching more than one eligible key is rejected as ambiguous
items.detail: No selection by array order. Keys are also filtered by use and by the algorithms the profile allows.

applicability.reason: Selecting a verification key by kid from a key set is part of JWT verification.

items.title: The revocation bound is documented as a sum and measured end to end
items.detail: Token lifetime plus key cache age plus introspection cache TTL plus any gateway cache. During a key endpoint outage the key cache term can grow as far as the staleness limit, after which every token is rejected. Disable an account and time how long requests keep succeeding.

applicability.reason: The bound adds token lifetime and key cache age, which need verified JWTs, to introspection cache time, which needs OAuth tokens, so either is enough.

items.title: Rejection responses do not say which check failed
items.detail: Callers get 401. The specific reason is logged internally with a correlation ID.

applicability.reason: Not telling a caller which authentication check failed is a readable requirement for any credential, so it stays visible whatever the system uses.

items.title: A logged value cannot forge or alter an entry
items.detail: Events are written by an encoder for a structured format. Test a value containing a line feed, a carriage return and the delimiter, and parse the log back.

applicability.reason: Any system that writes request values to a log can have an entry forged, whatever its architecture.

items.title: Event names and levels come from one documented vocabulary
items.detail: Every service uses the same name for the same event, so one rule covers all of them.

applicability.reason: A shared event vocabulary is a property of how any system logs, and no architecture fact removes the need for it.

items.title: Clocks are synchronised to a common source
items.detail: The allowed clock error is smaller than the shortest window any rule uses. Timestamps carry a UTC offset.

applicability.reason: Every system that timestamps events depends on its clocks, so synchronisation applies everywhere.

items.title: The iss parameter is compared as a simple string
items.detail: Against an issuer recorded before the redirect, with no case folding, port elision, trailing-slash or percent-encoding normalisation applied first.

applicability.reason: The iss authorization response parameter and the issuer recorded before the redirect are OAuth client objects (RFC 9207), so the item cannot apply without OAuth.

items.title: The targeted protocol revision is recorded and reviewed
items.detail: MCP revisions are dated and change on backwards incompatible changes. A review against an older revision can be wrong rather than merely stale.

applicability.reason: A process item, but its text limits it to recording the MCP revision, which has no meaning unless the system runs or connects to an MCP server.

items.title: One inventory lists every model, adapter, dataset and package that is loaded
items.detail: Each entry has a digest or version and a licence, and the list is compared with what is running.

applicability.reason: The inventory includes packages, which every system loads, so it applies even where no model or dataset is present.

items.title: Supplier terms, privacy policies and licences are reviewed before adoption
items.detail: The review is repeated when the supplier's terms or security posture change.

applicability.reason: Suppliers, their terms and licences exist for hosted model providers, model hubs, datasets and ordinary packages alike, so no single fact can rule the review out.

items.title: Token endpoint errors use the defined codes and leak nothing else
items.detail: Responses do not reveal which check failed, whether a client exists, or whether a code was valid but expired.

applicability.reason: The token endpoint and its defined error codes belong to OAuth.

items.title: Refusals do not disclose existence
items.detail: The same status and body whether the object exists or not, consistently across the service, unless an exception is documented.

applicability.reason: How a refusal is worded matters for any API with objects owned by different callers.

items.title: Identifiers are unguessable, and nothing depends on that
items.detail: Random values raise the cost of discovery. Removing the check because identifiers are UUIDs is not a trade, it is the vulnerability.

applicability.reason: Identifier choice and the ownership check behind it apply to any API with objects owned by different callers.

items.title: Untrusted content is fenced with a per-request nonce
items.detail: A fixed delimiter is a string the document can contain, and then the content after it reads as though it came from you.

applicability.reason: Fencing untrusted content inside a prompt needs a model that is given a prompt, whatever the source of that content.

items.title: No input filter is reported as coverage
items.detail: If one exists, the review records the phrasings it covers and that the list is not coverage.

applicability.reason: An input filter against prompt injection, and how it is reported, only matters where a model processes input.

items.title: Counters are held in a store every instance shares
items.detail: Tested by driving traffic through two instances. Local counters multiply the published limit by the instance count.

applicability.reason: Where rate limit counters live is a question for any API with a limit, and no fact records how many instances run.

items.title: The worst-case burst is written down and matches the algorithm
items.detail: A fixed window permits twice the limit across its boundary. A token bucket permits its capacity. Test the boundary.

applicability.reason: Any API with a rate limit has a worst-case burst set by its algorithm, whatever the architecture.

items.title: 429 responses are uncacheable and cheap
items.detail: RFC 6585 requires they not be stored by a cache, and permits dropping instead when answering is itself the cost.

applicability.reason: Any API that refuses on a rate limit sends 429 responses, whatever the architecture.

items.title: The parser refuses NaN and Infinity
items.detail: Neither is valid JSON. Python's json module accepts them by default. Check your library's default and use its strict setting.

applicability.reason: Any API that parses JSON can be handed NaN or Infinity, and no fact describes the body format.

items.title: String and array fields have per-field maximum lengths
items.detail: A single global limit sized for the largest field is no limit for the rest.

applicability.reason: String and array fields exist in almost any API, and per-field length limits do not depend on any architecture fact.

items.title: Rejections name the rule and do not echo the value
items.detail: One status, one error shape, no attacker-controlled bytes in logs or responses.

applicability.reason: Every API rejects some requests, so how a rejection is worded and logged applies everywhere.

items.title: RelayState is never followed as a URL without validation
items.detail: It is an opaque handle looked up in the session, or it is matched against an allowlist of the application's own paths. An unknown value leads to a default page.
items.lesson: SAML assertions and where they meet APIs

applicability.reason: RelayState is a SAML binding parameter, so the item needs SAML.

items.title: Neither responses nor refusal reasons reach the caller unchanged
items.detail: One status, no detail. "Address literal, private" tells the caller which rule refused them.
items.lesson: SSRF and unsafe consumption of APIs

applicability.reason: The item has two parts, and passing an upstream response back unchanged matters for any outbound request, including one to a fixed address.

items.title: The last TLS termination before the service is named, and what crosses it is stated
items.detail: Anything past it is a separate trust relationship whether or not it was designed as one.

applicability.reason: Every service receives its traffic past some TLS termination, even when that termination is the service itself, so naming it applies to every review.

items.title: For each value in a request, who can produce it and who can check it is written down
items.detail: Where the two sets are the same, the design records that the receiver can forge and that this was accepted.

applicability.reason: Writing down who can produce and who can check each request value is a design review step that applies to any API, whatever credentials it uses.

items.title: No error response carries a stack trace, query text, file path or version
items.detail: One global handler returns a generic body with a correlation ID, and the detail is logged on the server under the same ID.

applicability.reason: Any API can raise an error, so what an error response reveals is checkable on every system.

items.title: Each route allows only the methods it needs
items.detail: Everything else returns 405 with an Allow header and has no effect. TRACE is off.

applicability.reason: Every API has routes and methods, so a method allowlist per route applies to all systems.

items.title: Every environment is built from one baseline and audited automatically
items.detail: The audit compares settings with the baseline and probes the running service. The list of settings allowed to differ is short and reviewed.

applicability.reason: Every system is deployed in at least one environment that can drift from its baseline, and the item describes how that is audited.

items.title: The revocation bound is unchanged and still stated
items.detail: A bound token remains valid until it expires unless active state is consulted. Module 6's sum still applies.

applicability.reason: The item is about how long a bound token stays valid after withdrawal, which presupposes bound tokens.

items.title: The permission filter is applied to the corpus, not the result
items.detail: Post-filtering returns fewer results than requested, which discloses removals, and lets other tenants outrank the caller's own documents.

applicability.reason: Filtering before ranking applies to any search over resources of different tenants, with or without a model, and multi-tenant resources are deliberately not a fact.

items.title: Every number in a retrieval response is computed after the filter
items.detail: A total computed before it confirms that documents the caller may not read exist.

applicability.reason: A count that reveals documents the caller may not read is a cross-tenant authorization leak in any search response, not only in retrieval for a model.

items.title: No ranking adjustment is reported as a security control
items.detail: State the margin it changes. In the lab it was 0.08 to 0.06, with the order unchanged.

applicability.reason: Ranking adjustments are a property of a retrieval index feeding a model, so the item needs retrieval.

items.title: Written permission and scope exist before any security test is sent
items.detail: Signed by the system's owner, naming what is in scope, what is excluded, the dates and a contact. Third-party systems are tested only with their owner's written consent.

applicability.reason: Permission and scope are needed before any security test of any system, whatever its architecture.

items.title: Tests run in a test environment, with test data, at an agreed rate
items.detail: Any real data a test returns is recorded as reachable and not copied. Findings and test logs are handled as sensitive.

applicability.reason: Where and how tests are run is a matter of test process that applies to every review.

items.title: Every control has negative tests, not only functional ones
items.detail: For each operation there is at least one request that must be refused, and the suite fails when a known flaw is planted.

applicability.reason: Every API has operations with requests that must be refused, so negative tests apply to every system.

items.title: What is deployed is compared with what is described
items.detail: From a probe and from the route table, in both directions. An operation that answers and is not described is a finding, and gets the same tests as the rest.

applicability.reason: Comparing what is deployed with what is described is an inventory step that applies to every API.

items.title: Business rules have tests written by someone who knows the rule
items.detail: Each flow that costs something when repeated, reordered or exceeded has a misuse case and a test. Generated tests do not cover these.

applicability.reason: Business rules and state-changing flows exist in almost every API, and this is a statement about how tests are written.

items.title: A test run is checked against the logs and alerts
items.detail: The refusals the test caused appear in the log with the right account, and the detection rules that should fire did.

applicability.reason: Checking a test run against logs and alerts is a test process step that applies to every review.

items.title: Each finding can be repeated and stays in the build as a test
items.detail: It records the request, the expected and observed results, the control that failed and how to re-test, and the stored request runs on every change.

applicability.reason: How findings are recorded and kept as regression tests applies to every review.

items.title: The report states what was tested, what was not, and what a clean result means
items.detail: Scope, build, accounts and cases are listed. A clean result is reported as the cases run being refused, never as the absence of flaws.

applicability.reason: What the test report states applies to every test, whatever the system looks like.

items.title: The version list comes from the network and is dated
items.detail: Every deployment that answers, not every version in the documentation. Compare the two and act on the difference.

applicability.reason: Producing the list of answering deployments from the network is how extra versions are found, so it cannot depend on already knowing there are any.

items.title: Every superseded version has both dates, in the required order
items.detail: RFC 9745 forbids a sunset earlier than the deprecation. Check it in the build; the two dates usually come from different people.

applicability.reason: A superseded version exists only where more than one version does or did.

items.title: Deprecated versions emit Deprecation, Sunset and a Link
items.detail: Verified against a live response, not a design document.

applicability.reason: Deprecated versions, as the lesson uses the term, are superseded ones, so the item needs more than one version to exist or to have existed.

items.title: Remaining callers are named for every version with traffic
items.detail: A version with traffic and no identified callers cannot be withdrawn, which is why it never is.

applicability.reason: Naming remaining callers is what lets an old version be withdrawn, so the item needs more than one version to exist or to have existed.

items.title: Internal and non-production versions are in the same inventory
items.detail: These are the ones missing from the documentation, which is why they last longest.

applicability.reason: Internal and non-production deployments are the ones a team does not count as versions, so this inventory check has to be shown to everyone.

items.title: Withdrawal is verified from the network afterwards
items.detail: The same way reachability was established in the first place.

applicability.reason: Checking that a withdrawn version stopped answering needs a version that was withdrawn, which means an older version has existed.

items.title: The documentation, the inventory, the route table and observed traffic are compared on a schedule
items.detail: Every version on one list and not on another has a finding: answering with no record (a shadow API), or answering after it was recorded as retired or passed its sunset date (a zombie API).

applicability.reason: Comparing the four lists is how undocumented and supposedly retired versions are found, so it cannot depend on knowing they exist.

items.title: Every inventory entry names an owner and points at the version's specification
items.detail: NIST SP 800-228 recommends that the inventory hold each API's specification, ownership information and runtime information. An entry with no owner is a version nobody will withdraw.

applicability.reason: An inventory entry with an owner and a specification is needed even for an API with a single version.

items.title: A duplicate gets the same response as the original
items.detail: RFC 8935 requires it. A different response breaks honest retries and reveals which identifiers exist.

applicability.reason: Answering a duplicate event like the original is a rule for a receiver of pushed events, so it needs inbound webhooks.

items.title: Handlers tolerate out-of-order delivery
items.detail: Or the design states why order is guaranteed. Delivery is at least once and unordered.

applicability.reason: Out-of-order delivery is a property of webhook events, so the item needs handlers that receive them.

items.title: The register has been reconciled against the systems, and the date is published
items.detail: Both directions of the difference are reported. An unreconciled register is a record of what was remembered, and any clean report from it means nothing.

applicability.reason: Reconciling a credential register against the systems is an inventory step that applies whatever kinds of credential the system uses.

items.title: Every credential has an owning team, never an individual
items.detail: Reassignment is a normal operation. If the only honest answer is a person, that is the finding.

applicability.reason: Any system that holds a service credential of any kind needs an owner for it, and no single fact covers every kind of credential.

items.title: Every credential has a rotation interval and a last-rotated date
items.detail: Both halves. Overdue ones are named and assigned, not counted.

applicability.reason: Rotation applies to every long-lived credential a system holds, including kinds that no single fact names.

items.title: Every credential has a retirement condition recorded at issue
items.detail: A date or a named event. Pilots, migrations and single-partner integrations get the end of that thing.

applicability.reason: A recorded end condition is needed for every kind of credential, so no architecture fact rules it out.

facts.question: Does any caller authenticate by presenting a static key or other long-lived shared secret as it is?
Does any caller sign its requests, with a shared secret (HMAC) or a private key (HTTP message signatures)?
Does the system issue, obtain or accept OAuth 2.0 access tokens, as an authorization server, a client or a resource server?
Does the system verify any JSON Web Token: an access token, an ID token or an assertion?
Are any access tokens bound to a key the client must prove it holds (DPoP, or certificate-bound tokens with mutual TLS)?
Does the system sign people in with OpenID Connect, as a relying party or as a provider?
Does the system accept or issue SAML assertions?
Does the system itself expose authentication or account-recovery endpoints for people, such as login, registration, password reset or an MFA challenge?
Is the API called from a web browser, by a page the team owns or by anyone else's?
Does a browser authenticate to the system with a cookie it attaches automatically?
Does any service rely on a separate gateway, proxy, load balancer or edge component for security or identity context used when handling requests?
Does one software service call another software service's API, whether the other service is internal or external to the system boundary?
Does a service call another service on behalf of a user, carrying or exchanging that user's authority?
Does the system receive inbound webhook, callback, or push-notification deliveries from another party, including protocol features such as A2A push notifications?
Does the system make HTTP requests to other systems?
Can a caller, a tenant, or content the system processes influence the URL or host of a request the system makes?
Is more than one version of the API exposed, or has an older version ever been?
Does the system serve a GraphQL API?
Does the system serve a gRPC API?
Does the system accept WebSocket connections?
Does a language model process input anywhere in the system, whether hosted by a provider or run by the team?
Can a model's output cause an action: a tool call, an API call, a command, or a message to another agent?
Is code or a command that a model produced ever executed?
Is a model given content taken from a store: a document index, a vector store, or memory written in an earlier session?
Does the system run a Model Context Protocol server, or connect to one as a client?
Does the system take part in the Agent2Agent protocol, as a server or a client?

Does the team load, deploy or build from externally obtained model-related artifacts, such as models, adapters, tokenizers, datasets or serialized model files, rather than only calling a hosted model API?
